vopros: Should I pay for a tool that tracks whether ChatGPT and other AI assistants mention my business, or hire someone to get my business recommended by AI?

vyzhimka.tekst:
Probably not yet—unless AI assistants already influence a meaningful number of purchase decisions in your category.

I’d separate the two services:

- AI visibility tracking: useful for measurement, but I wouldn’t pay much just to know “ChatGPT mentioned us in 17% of prompts.” AI answers vary with the prompt, context, location, model, and whether web search is involved, so a single “share of AI voice” number can create false precision. ChatGPT itself can use current web sources when answering queries, which makes the underlying web presence particularly important. ([openai.com](https://openai.com/academy/search-and-deep-research/?utm_source=openai))
- “Get recommended by AI” consulting: potentially worthwhile, but be skeptical of anyone promising rankings or guaranteed recommendations. There isn't a magic submission process that makes ChatGPT recommend a company. OpenAI says public websites can appear in ChatGPT search and specifically recommends allowing OAI-SearchBot so content can be discovered and cited. ([help.openai.com](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/12627856?utm_source=openai))
- Traditional SEO/reputation/content work: this is where I would generally put money first. Google explicitly says its existing SEO fundamentals remain relevant to its generative AI results and says there aren't special technical requirements for appearing in AI Overviews or AI Mode. Its newer 2026 guidance similarly emphasizes valuable, distinctive content rather than some separate bag of “GEO” tricks. ([developers.google.com](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ai-features?authuser=50&utm_source=openai))

For a local business, for example, I'd rather have excellent Google/other relevant listings, lots of legitimate reviews, consistent business information, authoritative mentions, a crawlable website, good pages answering customers' actual questions, and clear evidence of what makes the business different. Those things are useful to humans, search engines, and AI systems rather than being an investment in one model's current behavior. Google explicitly recommends keeping business information current and taking advantage of things such as Business Profile and Merchant Center where relevant. ([developers.google.com](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/ai-optimization-guide?authuser=4&hl=en&utm_source=openai))

There is one increasingly good reason to track AI visibility, though: attribution. Google introduced dedicated generative-AI performance reporting in Search Console in 2026, making some of this measurable without buying a third-party monitoring platform. ([developers.google.com](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2026/06/gen-ai-performance-reports?utm_source=openai))

A practical rule: don't spend $1,000/month to improve an “AI visibility score” unless you can connect that score to leads or sales. Start by manually testing perhaps 20–50 high-intent questions a prospective customer would genuinely ask ChatGPT and other important assistants, such as “best X in Los Angeles,” “X vs Y,” or “who can help me with Z?” Record who gets recommended and, crucially, what sources the assistant relies upon. That usually reveals whether you actually have an AI-discovery problem and what needs fixing.

If you tell me what kind of business you run and roughly what you'd be asked to pay for the tracking/consulting, I can tell you whether I think it would be a sensible use of your marketing budget.
